files.synopsis:
Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 0: lifecycle vocabulary.

Every other package marks its elements with one of the keywords defined here, so a reader can tell what runs today from what docs/ROADMAP.md still owes. The model is one model; the keywords are the seam between "current" and "future".

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 1: requirements.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §0 read as a specification, plus the design rules the rest of the model has to satisfy and the promises it deliberately does not make. Ids in angle brackets are stable; the roadmap and assurance packages cite them.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 2: structure.

The shape of the system (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §1), the workspace it is built from (§9), the architecture facade, and the three architectures behind it. Subsystem internals live in the packages that follow; this one says what exists and how it is connected.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 3: boot.

The hand-off ABI, the two address layouts, the loader's sequence, the kernel's bring-up with every stage's self-check to stage 12, and the trap path. All of this runs today on all three architectures.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 4: memory.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4. The physical allocator, the heap, the page-table arithmetic and the kernel arena since stage 2; VMOs, process address spaces, demand paging and copy-on-write since stage 6, file mappings since stage 8. Reclaim is stage 13's and not built.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 5: processors, time, and scheduling.

Stages 3 to 5 run today: interrupts, a clock, every processor online, IPIs, TLB shootdown, grace periods, fair locks, and tasks scheduled by EEVDF in one Throughput domain. Stage 14's real-time domains are designed here (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5) and not yet written.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 6: kernel objects and the two ABIs.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2 and §3. The constants for the Linux half are in src/lib/proto/linux-abi and for the native half in src/lib/proto/native-abi. The objects a handle can name exist in src/kernel/src/object, the core half of a process among them; the POSIX half and threads in src/kernel/src/syscall. No handle names an address space or a thread yet.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 7: isolation.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6: namespaces, cgroups v2, seccomp, credentials. Stage 13, designed in from the start so that no global table has to be found later. The credentials exist since stage 7, and cgroup v2 since 2026-09-23 (docs/CGROUPS.md), over the job tree. Of the namespaces, mount namespaces are in (docs/NAMESPACES.md, N1 to N3): unshare and clone copy one, and bubblewrap runs as root. The other kinds still answer as a Linux built without them does, and setns refuses. Seccomp is not built.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 8: devices and userspace drivers.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §7. The kernel enumerates buses because that needs ACPI or a device tree and privileged access; it does not drive devices. Everything from the device node outward is stage 10, which is done: the drivers are processes devmgr starts. What it still owes is named on the part that owes it.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 9: storage.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §8. Block core, VFS, the small in-kernel filesystems and btrfs in three stages. What exists today is marked on each part.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 10: the roadmap.

docs/ROADMAP.md as requirements: one per stage, each with its exit criterion, its status, the boot test that verifies it, and the part of the system that satisfies or will satisfy it. Each stage's status keyword says whether it is done; docs/ROADMAP.md's "Where it stands" is the prose this follows.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 11: assurance.

docs/RELIABILITY.md and docs/ASSEMBLY.md: the quality gates, what each one verifies, and what the tests can actually reach. The gates cargo xtask check runs are in CI. Of the xtask boot gates, CI runs test-boot and test-rustc; the ones that need a binary the repository does not carry, a disk judged on the host or a screendump run in the landing gates of docs/BACKLOG.md instead (docs/ROADMAP.md, Continuously).

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 12: views.

How to read the one model as two: what runs today, and what the roadmap still owes. The filters key on the lifecycle keywords every element carries.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 13: the certified item's requirements.

The high-level requirements of the certified item (the `core` and `item` rings of docs/certification/ITEM.md): what each subsystem promises at its interface, decomposed from the Security Target's objectives (docs/certification/SECURITY-TARGET.md §4.1 and §8.2) and the safety manual's assumed safety requirements (SAFETY-MANUAL.md §2). The low-level requirements, one per unit of code, go in one file per subsystem after this one. docs/certification/IMPLEMENTATION.md W-8 is the design, and tools/common/check/check-traceability.py the gate that reads these and writes docs/certification/TRACEABILITY.md.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 14: the low-level requirements of object/.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/object/ does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format): the core ring's object layer -- what a handle names and how it is dropped, channels, ports, interrupts, I/O mappings, pins, the job quotas, jobs, the core half of a process, and the scoped OOM kill. The handle table itself and the rights arithmetic are `src/lib/kernel/objects` and `src/lib/proto/native-abi`, whose host tests verify H.OBJ.1 to H.OBJ.4 directly; nothing here restates them.

This is W-8's pilot (docs/certification/IMPLEMENTATION.md, step 3), the subsystem the format was corrected on before the others copy it. What it settled:

- one requirement per behaviour a check can pass or fail, and a requirement names every function that carries the behaviour as its `unit`, not one each: a write that is all or nothing is one sentence whatever number of functions make it so; - a requirement is no broader than one check can prove: a `Verifies:` tag credits the whole requirement, so every check that names one proves its whole criterion alone. Where the checks that exist each prove a part, the requirement is split, one part per check, and a part no check proves stays in the baseline as check-writing work -- never a tag crediting what its check does not test. The statement says no more than the criterion tests; - an accessor -- one statement or one expression, no branch and no `unsafe` -- needs no requirement of its own (check-traceability.py's rule); one is still named where it is the behaviour's entry point; - check code that lives in a product file is listed in tools/common/data/traceability-units.json, not given a requirement, and the requirement it would verify waits in the baseline until it moves into a check file where a `Verifies:` tag may go on it.

Ids are `L.object.<n>`, numbered through the subsystem; the package gives the file.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 15: the low-level requirements of sched/.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/sched/ does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format, part 14's pilot settled how they are cut). The scheduling decision itself is `src/lib/kernel/sched`'s `RunQueue`, an EEVDF queue the kernel's per-processor queue wraps; its host tests are the checks, and each requirement names the kernel function that carries the behaviour into the item as its `unit`.

The slice starts with the two requirements FX-0502's fix created. The rest of sched/ is check-writing work, in the baseline until then.

Ids are `L.sched.<n>`, numbered through the subsystem.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 16: the low-level requirements of iommu.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/iommu.rs and src/kernel/src/iommu/ does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format): where firmware puts each PCI function's DMA, the units the kernel turns translation on for, the domains a driver pins pages into, the gate a wait on a unit is made through, and the faults a unit records. The pins a program makes through a handle, and the quarantine a dead driver's pins go to, are object/'s (part 14, `L.object.45` to `L.object.49`); this is the domain side under them.

The format is the object/ pilot's (W-8 step 3), and so are its rules: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour as its `unit`; one check proves a whole requirement, so a requirement is split where the checks that exist each prove a part; a statement says no more than its criterion tests; an accessor needs no requirement of its own.

What proves what. The boot's own checks are in iommu/check.rs (the domain check, the fault audit, the unit gate), service_check.rs (a fault's words, a second domain, a dropped domain) and object/check.rs (a page pinned twice). Most of what a unit does is proved only end to end, by the out-of-domain probe in pci/virtio.rs: its device writes a page its domain does not map, and it counts the write as faulted only when the unit's record reads back as exactly that write by the domain's stream. pci/virtio.rs is product code, so the tag is on what judges the count, `xtask test-boot`'s `fault_problem`, and on x86-64 and AArch64 only: ARMv7-A programs no unit (AoU-6). What no check proves waits in the baseline as check-writing work; docs/certification/IMPLEMENTATION.md W-8 lists it.

Ids are `L.iommu.<n>`, numbered through the subsystem; the package gives the part of it.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 17: the low-level requirements of memory.

What each unit of the item's memory management does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format, part 14 is the pilot this copies), in two id spaces.

- `L.mm.<n>`: the kernel's own memory -- src/kernel/src/mm.rs and mm/ (the frame allocator's glue, the heap, the kernel's page tables, the allocation reserve, page tables unlinked and waiting for their shootdown), vmap.rs (the kernel address arena, device windows and kernel stacks) and early.rs (the mapper stage 1 runs before there is an allocator); - `L.user.<n>`: what a program's memory is made of -- src/kernel/src/user/ vmo.rs (memory objects: their pages, copy-on-write, sharing and retirement) and user/space.rs (address spaces: mappings, faults, protection, unmapping and its shootdown, and the charge for them).

Two id spaces rather than one, because they are two layers: nothing in `L.user` is reached before the kernel's own memory is up, and a check of a user address space is not evidence for the kernel's. Ids are flat within each, the package gives the file, and they are never renumbered once a check names them.

The frame, heap, paging and vma arithmetic itself is src/lib/kernel/frame, heap, paging and vma, whose host tests verify it; nothing here restates them. What is here is what the kernel does with them.

The pilot's rules hold: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour; it is no broader than one check can prove, and where the checks that exist each prove a part it is split; an accessor needs no requirement of its own; and check code living in a product file is listed in tools/common/data/traceability-units.json, not required.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 18: the low-level requirements of the x86-64 architecture, the trap path and the system call entry.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/, src/kernel/src/trap.rs and src/kernel/src/syscall/mod.rs's dispatcher does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format): the descriptor tables and which selectors ring 3 may hold, the context switch and the user state it carries, starting processors, the paranoid entries, the speculation defences, the counter and timer, both ABIs' signal frames, SYSCALL and int $0x80, the exception gates and what a fault becomes, and which calls reach which answer.

The format is the object/ pilot's (W-8 step 3), and so are its rules: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour as its `unit`; one check proves a whole requirement, so a requirement is split where the checks that exist each prove a part; a statement says no more than its criterion tests; an accessor needs no requirement of its own.

What proves what. Most of this is proved by programs the boot runs in ring 3: arch/x86_64/trap/check.rs's faulting programs and its i386 programs (int $0x80, thread-local segments, both signal frames and a fork, forged frames, socketcall), syscall/check.rs's 64-bit ones, and paranoid/check.rs's breakpoints in the SYSCALL window. Two limits of the default gate are said where they matter: under TCG the processor offers no speculation controls and the counter is the HPET, so the read-back and the TSC paths are exercised by the KVM boot row only; and several checks the boot runs -- stage 3's breakpoints and demand paging, the timer's rate, CR0.WP -- are functions of main.rs, product code a tag cannot go on, so their requirements wait in the baseline until the checks move. So does every criterion no check tests: docs/certification/IMPLEMENTATION.md W-8 lists them.

Ids are `L.x86_64.<n>`, `L.trap.<n>` and `L.syscall.<n>`, numbered through each; the package gives the part.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 19: the low-level requirements of arch/aarch64.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/arch/aarch64/ does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format, part 14 is the pilot this copies): the trap path and the signal frames it builds, the context switch, the interrupt controllers and the generic timer, the boot console, the system registers, translation and the TLB, starting the other processors, the speculation defences, and what firmware is asked for -- power, reset, entropy. The PL011 and the GICv2 are arch/arm_common's, shared with ARMv7-A, and are not here.

What proves what. This architecture's own checks are arch/aarch64/check.rs (the machine check: exception syndromes decoded, console= values, the TRNG against scripted firmware, the GIC's driver per description, masking read back at the controller, refusals, a system call rewound), arch/aarch64/trap/check.rs (real programs whose own instructions fault, each required to end with the signal Linux sends) and arch/aarch64/speculation/check.rs (the part tables, firmware's answers, the entry loop's count). Most of the rest is exercised by every boot -- the console carries the log, the timer ticks, the secondaries start, the scheduler switches -- but through checks in product code (main.rs's stage checks) or through generic checks whose criteria are the generic layer's, so it waits in the baseline as check-writing work rather than being credited to a check that does not assert it. Where the hardware a unit drives is not on the machine the suite boots -- the crosvm guest's 16550, the Pixel 7's ramoops zone and watchdogs, a firmware TRNG -- the criterion says which machine shows it.

Ids are `L.aarch64.<n>`, flat through the architecture; the package gives the area. The pilot's rules hold: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour; it is no broader than one check can prove; an accessor needs no requirement of its own; and check code living in a product file is listed in tools/common/data/traceability-units.json.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 20: the low-level requirements of a device's claim, its node, and its quiesce.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/claim.rs and src/kernel/src/device.rs does, and the quiesce in src/kernel/src/syscall/native.rs, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format): a device claimed through its core's control channels, the number its node is published under, the apertures and vectors a node hands out and nothing past them, the MSI-X vectors it mints, the bus mastering a quiesce turns off, and the quiesce itself, which waits out every core that serves the device before the next driver is given it. The objects a driver holds for a device -- its mapping, its interrupt, its pins -- are object/'s (part 14); the domain under them is iommu's (part 16).

The format and its rules are the object/ pilot's (W-8 step 3): a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour as its `unit`; one check proves a whole requirement; a statement says no more than its criterion tests; an accessor needs no requirement of its own.

What proves what. The claims and numbers are proved by service_check.rs, on claims of its own. A node's rules are proved on every boot, before the nodes are published, by device/check.rs, which `device::publish` runs. The quiesce is proved by block_ring/check.rs, which drives `device_quiesce` through a driver's life and death on the first PCI function, and by xtask's `test-init`, which restarts `devmgr`. What no check proves waits in the baseline as check-writing work.

Ids are `L.claim.<n>`, `L.device.<n>` and `L.quiesce.<n>`, numbered through each part; `L.quiesce` names the behaviour, whose units are in syscall/native.rs.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 21: the low-level requirements of arch/armv7a, as far as they are written.

ARMv7-A, the Cortex-A7 of the STM32MP157, has no requirements of its own beyond these: what the system call path does for the filter the core asks about every call (seccomp, `docs/SECCOMP.md` §3.3), and what its switch barrier does inside a speculation domain (`docs/OPAQUE-KERNEL.md` §9). The rest of the architecture waits in the baseline with the other architectures' unwritten rows. Ids are `L.armv7a.<n>`, flat through the architecture; the rules of part 19 hold.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 22: the low-level requirements of smp.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/smp.rs does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format, part 14 is the pilot this copies): finding the processors and giving each a record it finds itself by, starting the secondaries, the inter-processor interrupt, the TLB shootdown -- whole and scoped, and the bound on how long it waits -- grace periods, stopping the other processors for a panic, and the scheduler's kick. The start sequences themselves, the per-processor register and the interrupt controller are each architecture's (src/kernel/src/arch/<isa>/smp.rs), and belong to the arch slices; this is the architecture-independent half above them.

The pilot's rules hold: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour as its `unit`; one check proves a whole requirement, so a requirement is no broader than one check can prove; a statement says no more than its criterion tests; an accessor needs no requirement of its own; check code living in a product file is listed in tools/common/data/traceability-units.json, not required -- here `run_everywhere` and `next_job`, the way stage 4's checks hand work to every processor, which nothing else uses.

What proves what. Stage 4's checks in smp/check.rs run on every processor at once: `everywhere` (100 rounds of work, each processor's record against its hardware, the interrupts the secondaries took), `page_sets`, `tables_wait_for_their_shootdown`, `shootdown` (a page moved under every processor 20 times), `grace`, and after the scheduler starts `migrating_shootdown`. The scoped shootdown reaching another processor is proved from user mode by user/rmap_check.rs's protect step. The bound on a wait for a processor that never answers is proved only by the negative control recorded in commit 94dee288, a scratch edit that made one processor stop answering, and the bound on the shootdown turn by nothing at all (commit 237d2426 says why): no boot check makes a processor stuck, because the boot test counts the panic that follows as a failure. They wait in the baseline with the rest of what no check proves; docs/certification/IMPLEMENTATION.md W-8 lists it.

Ids are `L.smp.<n>`, numbered through the subsystem; the package gives the part of it. They are never renumbered once a check names them.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 23: the low-level requirements of console.

What each unit of src/kernel/src/console.rs and src/kernel/src/console/ does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format, part 14 is the pilot this copies): the kernel's lines to the port, whole and in order; the way a failure report gets past a lock nobody will release; the recent-output ring a panic screen draws; the transmit ring and the writers who queue into it, wait for room or poll; the receive ring the port's interrupt fills; the kernel log every byte is recorded in, what it promises a reader and what it keeps out; and the boot console drawn on the framebuffer. The ports themselves are each architecture's (src/kernel/src/arch/<isa>/console.rs) and belong to the arch slices; the two of their functions that decide *which* console the kernel writes to, and whose checks test that, are here too (`Ports`), at the coordinator's asking.

The pilot's rules hold: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour as its `unit`; one check proves a whole requirement, so a requirement is no broader than one check can prove; a statement says no more than its criterion tests; an accessor needs no requirement of its own; check code living in a product file is listed in tools/common/data/traceability-units.json, not required -- here `console::input::check` and `console::output::check`, which read their rings' private state and so cannot move to a check file without becoming child modules. Until they do, the requirements they prove (`L.console.9`, `.10` and `.20`) wait in the baseline.

What proves what. console/log_check.rs (FX-0505, the `log` line) drives rings of its own through wrap, overrun, a partial read and two racing writers, and then requires of the kernel log that a task's write and a line written as a failure report are in it and a line sent unlogged is not. service_check.rs reads back the recent-output ring. xtask's `test-init-file` ends a boot in the FX-1501 panic and requires its line on the port. arch/aarch64/check.rs reads and refuses `console=ramoops,...` values, and arch/armv7a/check.rs holds the console a device tree chooses to the port it must be. Nothing tests a report written while the port's lock is held for good, the transmit ring full, a stalled port or the screen console; docs/certification/IMPLEMENTATION.md W-8 lists them.

Ids are `L.console.<n>`, numbered through the subsystem; the package gives the part of it. They are never renumbered once a check names them.

Ferrix — SysML v2 model, part 24: the low-level requirements of btrfs.

What each unit of the two btrfs crates in the item does, as `ItemLowLevel` requirements (part 13 defines the format, part 14 is the pilot this copies): `ferrix-btrfs` (src/lib/fs/btrfs), the reader, and `ferrix-btrfs-write` (src/lib/fs/btrfs-write), the write path. They joined the item on 2026-10-02 (the customer's decision; ITEM.md). Their interface below is the `Device` and `WriteDevice` traits, which the kernel's block layer answers; above, `Volume` and `WriteVolume`, which the VFS glue in the load (`ferrix-btrfs-vfs`, src/kernel/src/fs/btrfs*.rs) calls. A unit is named from the crate's src/, led by the crate's name: `ferrix_btrfs::volume::Volume::read_node`.

The pilot's rules hold: a requirement names every function that carries its behaviour as its `unit`; one check proves a whole requirement, so a requirement is no broader than one check can prove; a statement says no more than its criterion tests; an accessor needs no requirement of its own. The first version of this part, L.btrfs.1 to 23, broke the second rule: many of them were conjunctions whose clauses different tests proved. The certification consultant found it (2026-10-02). Each was narrowed to what one test proves, and every clause it gave up that a test proves became a requirement of its own, L.btrfs.24 to 107; ids a check named were not renumbered. Clauses no test proved were dropped rather than kept unverified: the commit's settling bound (64 passes), and a reload whose own log replay aborts (docs/BACKLOG.md).

What proves what. Every check here is a host test of the crates themselves, against images `mkfs.btrfs` made (src/lib/fs/btrfs/testdata) and against a device in memory that records every write and flush, so that a crash can be rebuilt from the record; except L.btrfs.21, 105, 106 and 107, whose tests drive the write path through the load's `ferrix-btrfs-vfs`, because a mount is where ENOSPC and a read-only reload show. The `btrfs_read` fuzzer (src/tests/fuzz) exercises the reader beyond these and is not a verifier the gate reads. Nothing fuzzes the write path.

Written and not yet verified, so in the baseline: L.btrfs.9 and L.btrfs.12, the volumes the reader and the writer refuse to open, which no test opens; and L.btrfs.23, arithmetic that cannot overflow, which a lint would enforce and none does yet (the certification consultant's advice, 2026-10-02).

Ids are `L.btrfs.<n>`, numbered through both crates; the package gives the part. They are never renumbered once a check names them.

packages.name: FerrixLifecycle
packages.doc:
Four maturities and the stage that owns an element.

#implemented   the code exists and a QEMU boot exercises it on every architecture it applies to: the boot test itself, or a named `cargo xtask test-*` gate. #inProgress    the owning stage has started; part of the element runs. #writtenAhead  a `src/lib/` crate exists and passes its host tests, but no gate exercises it yet through the kernel or a program in the image. #planned       only the design exists, in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

`@stage { number = n; }` names the docs/ROADMAP.md stage that owns the element. An element with no stage is cross-cutting.

children.name: stage
children.doc: The roadmap stage, 0 to 22, that owns the element.

children.name: deferred
children.doc: Work a finished stage explicitly left behind, with the reason the stage gave. Deferred is not the same as planned: the stage that owns it is closed, and the item waits for a machine, a workload or a later stage to make it meaningful.

children.name: GoalRequirement
children.doc: A requirement the acceptance test forces. Every one of these is load-bearing: it is why the system is shaped the way it is, and why toy-OS shortcuts are ruled out at the start rather than discovered to be dead ends at the end.

children.name: hostsRustc
children.doc: The acceptance test: a statically linked musl `rustc` compiles `hello.rs` on Ferrix, the binary it produced runs, and CI proves both. Not "has a shell", not "draws a window". Hosting a compiler is the hardest thing a general-purpose OS is routinely asked to do and the only goal that forces every subsystem to be real.

children.name: kernelThreads
children.doc: rustc needs clone(CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_VM|CLONE_SETTLS), the futex family, set_tid_address and robust lists. Forces: 1:1 kernel threads, a real futex, per-thread TLS registers.

children.name: addressSpaceScale
children.doc: mmap/mprotect/munmap with MAP_FIXED and MAP_NORESERVE over 2 to 8 GiB of address space. Forces: demand paging, a VMA tree, lazy anonymous memory, overcommit.

children.name: signalDelivery
children.doc: A SIGSEGV handler on an alternate stack. Forces: real signal delivery, sigaltstack, rt_sigreturn.

children.name: processSpawn
children.doc: fork/execve/wait4 to run the linker. Forces: copy-on-write fork, an ELF loader, process groups, exit status plumbing.

children.name: syscallSurface
children.doc: openat, getdents64, statx, renameat2, pread64, about 150 syscalls in total. Forces: a VFS with inode and dentry caches.

children.name: procfs
children.doc: /proc/self/maps, /proc/self/exe, /proc/self/fd. Forces: a procfs backed by the real VM and fd table.

children.name: durableFilesystem
children.doc: A writable filesystem with room for a ~2 GiB sysroot. Forces: a block stack and an on-disk filesystem that survives a crash.

children.name: memoryPressure
children.doc: rustc will exhaust memory on a small machine, so reclaim is a correctness requirement: an OOM kill scoped by Job and cgroup, never a livelock.

children.name: selfHosting
children.doc: Stage 20: build Ferrix on Ferrix. The image the Ferrix-hosted compiler produces boots and passes every boot test.

children.name: Principles
children.doc: Decisions that shape every subsystem. They are requirements because the assurance package verifies most of them with a script or a build failure rather than a review.

children.name: linuxIsTheNativeAbi
children.doc: Syscall 0 is `read`. The Linux syscall ABI is the native interface, not a compatibility layer, so the static-musl world is the userland from the first day there is one, and POSIX conformance is inherited rather than reimplemented. The alternative — a native target with its own std — needs LLVM built for it, which drags a C++ runtime into the tree.

children.name: monolithicCoreCapabilitySeams
children.doc: A syscall is a function call, not four IPC hops. Device drivers run as user processes holding capabilities, so a driver fault is a process fault. The line is drawn at devices: filesystems and the page cache stay in the kernel because rustc touches them on every path.

children.name: oneInKernelDevice
children.doc: The one in-kernel device is a serial port writer, for early boot and panic output when no userspace exists. Named as an exception so that it stays one.

children.name: nothingStubbed
children.doc: Nothing is stubbed that a later stage has to unpick: no fixed-size process table, no in-memory-only filesystem, no cooperative scheduler.

children.name: pureFunctionsInLibs
children.doc: Anything expressible as a pure function of bytes goes to `src/lib/`, and gets a fuzz target and a Miri run, before the kernel calls it. That is the only code cargo test, Miri and the fuzzers can reach.

children.name: oneArchFacade
children.doc: Generic code never names an architecture and #[cfg(target_arch)] appears nowhere outside arch/. Enforced by tools/common/check/check-crate-layering.sh, because a facade maintained by convention is a facade for about six weeks.

children.name: assemblyOnlyWhereTheMachineDefinesIt
children.doc: No assembly at boot on any architecture. What exists is confined to constructs the machine defines before a Rust function could run, listed in tools/common/data/asm-allowlist.json with an argument each, under an absolute line cap.

children.name: oneLayoutPerAddressWidth
children.doc: The 64-bit pair share identical layout constants; ARMv7-A has a 32-bit layout that is argued rather than merely different. Both are checked at compile time on every build.

children.name: namespacesDesignedIn
children.doc: All eight namespaces from the start: every global table is reached through the task's NsSet from the first line, so nobody has to find those tables years later.

children.name: iommuIsNotOptional
children.doc: A userspace driver without an IOMMU can write any physical address, which is worse than an in-kernel driver. Where no IOMMU exists, drivers run in a degraded trusted mode and the kernel says so loudly at boot.

children.name: everyStageEndsInSomethingThatRuns
children.doc: A stage's exit criterion is a QEMU boot that demonstrates the new capability and stays in CI forever after.

children.name: unsafeIsExpensive
children.doc: unsafe is not forbidden, it is made expensive: a SAFETY comment on every block, one unsafe operation per block, a Safety section on every unsafe fn, and a script in CI so a softened clippy lint cannot retire the rule.

children.name: noReachablePanic
children.doc: panic!, unreachable!, unwrap, expect and unchecked indexing are denied in production code; every exemption is an #[expect] whose reason begins AUDIT:. A reachable panic is an unrecoverable machine. A fatal condition in the kernel is fatal!, which names the catalog entry that explains it and panics from inside the macro; a bare panic! is denied there as everywhere.

children.name: overflowChecksInRelease
children.doc: Overflow checks stay on in release. A wrapped frame number is a write to the wrong physical page whose symptom appears elsewhere; a panic that names the line is strictly better.

children.name: provedOnEveryBoot
children.doc: The kernel proves its invariants on every boot rather than asserting them: the memory map is checked, the direct map is checked to alias physical memory, the allocators are required to give every frame back.

children.name: oneAuthorPerCommit
children.doc: docs/CONVENTIONS.md: a commit names one author. No Co-authored-by trailer, no Generated-with line, no tool signature, whoever or whatever made the change; a message is a subject, a blank line, and a body that argues the why. This overrides any agent's default attribution instruction.

children.name: aGateNeedsNoArming
children.doc: A control that only runs once a clone has been configured is not a control. Two hooks behind one un-committable core.hooksPath switch were one control with two names, and neither fired while eight trailer-carrying commits were written. Every rule has a check in CI that needs no local setup and cannot be skipped with --no-verify; hooks are the convenience, CI is the guarantee.

children.name: noCertifiedWcet
children.doc: HardRt promises EDF with admission control, bounded kernel critical sections on the RT path, preallocated pools there, and interrupts that cannot steal unaccounted time. It does not promise a certified worst-case execution time for the whole kernel; no OS that also hosts LLVM can.

children.name: noRaid56
children.doc: btrfs is single-device to begin with and RAID 5/6 is out of scope; it is where btrfs itself is weakest.

children.name: noAml
children.doc: src/lib/platform/acpi reads the fixed tables only. There is no AML interpreter and there will be none.

children.name: FirmwareKind
children.doc: Every architecture boots via UEFI, so firmware calls a Rust efi_main with a stack set up and the MMU on. Which firmware differs: EDK2 on the 64-bit pair, U-Boot's bootefi on ARMv7-A (upstream EDK2 dropped its 32-bit Arm build, and U-Boot is what the STM32MP157 runs anyway).

children.name: MachineDescription
children.doc: How the kernel learns what the machine contains: ACPI tables on x86-64 and on AArch64 under EDK2, a flattened device tree on ARMv7-A and on AArch64 firmware that offers one.

children.name: hardwareId
children.doc: What the machine calls it: an APIC ID, or the affinity fields of MPIDR. Not dense, so the kernel also assigns a logical index; the boot CPU is always logical zero.

children.name: Iommu
children.doc: VT-d or AMD-Vi on x86-64, SMMUv3 on AArch64. Absent on QEMU's default machines, which is why the degraded trusted mode exists.

children.name: Machine
children.doc: The system context. Ferrix targets QEMU's q35 and virt machines in CI and the STM32MP157 on the ARMv7-A side.

children.name: EfiSystemTable
children.doc: Firmware's table: boot services, con_out, the configuration tables that carry the RSDP or the device tree.

children.name: EfiHandoffPort
children.doc: extern "efiapi" fn efi_main(image, system_table). On ARMv7-A the calling convention lowers to AAPCS on the musleabi target, so the signature is the same on all three.

children.name: BootHandoffPort
children.doc: The loader and the kernel are two programs linked for different targets that meet at exactly one struct, declared once in src/lib/proto/bootinfo. A mismatch is a type error rather than a triple fault.

children.name: SyscallResult
children.doc: A value, or a negative errno, exactly as Linux returns it.

children.name: LinuxSyscallPort
children.doc: Syscall numbers 0.., each architecture's table as Linux defines it (the EABI table on ARMv7-A). A compatibility obligation: no opinions live here. src/lib/proto/linux-abi holds the numbers, errnos and repr(C) layouts.

children.name: NativeSyscallPort
children.doc: Syscall numbers from 0x1000, capability-handle based. Where the design opinions live; what devmgr and drivers speak. A process may use both ports.

children.name: SerialConsolePort
children.doc: Early boot and panic output. The boot test reads this stream and waits for the marker FERRIX-BOOT-OK.

children.name: Ferrix
children.doc: An operating system written in Rust for x86-64, AArch64 and ARMv7-A, whose acceptance test is that it compiles Rust.

children.name: Deployment
children.doc: Ferrix on a machine. CI instantiates three of these under QEMU; the STM32MP157-DK board is the fourth, reached by `cargo xtask deploy --arch armv7a`, which copies two files onto a vendor-provisioned card rather than writing a whole image, because the board's boot chain lives in partitions imaging would destroy, then watches the ST-LINK serial port for the marker. It has run on hardware: an STM32MP157D-DK1 at two cores reached FERRIX-BOOT-OK stages 1-9 and ran stage 7's script at fd4442e.

children.name: ferrix
children.doc: The reference instance the roadmap and assurance packages point at.

children.name: Loader
children.doc: src/boot/common/uefi/: the UEFI loader. Reads the kernel from the volume it was booted from, copies it to its link address, builds the address space, takes the memory map, leaves boot services, installs the new tables and jumps. Only the last step is assembly, because the return address of a Rust call would be in the address space just replaced. One program for three architectures: src/boot/common/uefi/src/arch has one file per machine and no second loader.

children.name: uefi
children.doc: src/boot/common/uefi/src/uefi: the handful of protocols and tables used — simple file system, loaded image, graphics output, and the ACPI and device-tree configuration tables. Hand-written, no crates.io dependency.

children.name: services
children.doc: src/boot/common/uefi/src/services.rs: allocation, memory map, and the one call after which firmware is gone: ExitBootServices.

children.name: load
children.doc: src/boot/common/uefi/src/load.rs: ELF parse via src/lib/platform/elf, placement, page tables via src/lib/kernel/paging, the identity plan for the switch.

children.name: LoaderArch
children.doc: prepare_cpu, clean_dcache, enter_kernel: what each machine needs between ExitBootServices and the kernel's first instruction.

children.name: enterKernel
children.doc: The one assembly site in the loader. x86-64: EFER.NXE, CR4.PGE, write CR3, jump. AArch64: MMU off, MAIR/TCR/TTBR0/1, SCTLR, MMU on, jump — TCR cannot be reprogrammed under a live regime. ARMv7-A: the same through cp15, refusing to start in HYP mode rather than leaving it.

children.name: Kernel
children.doc: src/kernel/: monolithic core, capability seams, userspace device drivers. Entered from the loader with the MMU on, three mappings in place and nothing else: no vectors, no allocator, no other CPU running.

children.name: printer
children.doc: src/kernel/src/console.rs: println over the arch console, behind a lock that a panicking CPU waits a bounded time for, so a fault while printing still produces its FERRIX-PANIC line. It keeps its last 4 KiB in a lock-free ring, which a panic draws on the firmware framebuffer when there is one (src/kernel/src/panic/screen.rs): the second in-kernel output device, write-only and used for nothing else.

children.name: lockOrder
children.doc: mm.rs: TABLES serialises every walk and change of the kernel page tables and is taken before FRAMES (a mapping may need a frame for a table) and before HEAP (an unmap records what it released). Never the other way round. Stage 5 adds a run queue's lock outside the heap's and the frame allocator's, with nothing ever taken outside it.

children.name: Initramfs
children.doc: A cpio "newc" archive xtask writes and the loader reads from FERRIX/INITRD.IMG into memory nothing reclaims; the kernel unpacks it into the tmpfs root through the same VFS calls a program makes. It holds /sbin/devmgr, the drivers devmgr starts under /lib/drivers with a MANIFEST naming them, and /bin, whose shell since 2026-09-18 is zinc. What breaks the cycle "the root filesystem needs a block driver that lives on the root filesystem"; a btrfs root, on a boot that has one, is installed from the same archive (src/kernel/src/fs/root_disk.rs).

children.name: devmgr
children.doc: /sbin/devmgr, a native program on src/user/system/native/rt.

children.name: virtioBlk
children.doc: /lib/drivers/blk, a native program on src/user/system/native/rt.

children.name: virtioGpu
children.doc: /lib/drivers/gpu, a native program on src/user/system/native/rt.

children.name: virtioNet
children.doc: /lib/drivers/net, a native program on src/user/system/native/rt.

children.name: virtioInput
children.doc: /lib/drivers/input, a native program on src/user/system/native/rt.

children.name: vport
children.doc: /lib/drivers/vport, the virtio-serial port driver, a native program on src/user/system/native/rt.

children.name: virtioSndDriver
children.doc: /lib/drivers/snd, the virtio-snd driver (docs/AUDIO.md), a native program on src/user/system/native/rt over src/lib/drivers/sound/virtio-snd.

children.name: init
children.doc: The program the kernel starts first (src/kernel/src/init.rs): /bin/zinc unless a build names another with --init, or a list of commands run in turn.

children.name: UserProcess
children.doc: A running Linux binary -- static musl, a static PIE, or dynamically linked through the interpreter its PT_INTERP names -- as a Process (see FerrixObjects) speaking the Linux ABI, and optionally the native one. devmgr and the drivers are native programs on src/user/system/native/rt, which make the few Linux calls they need as well.

children.name: Userland
children.doc: Linux binaries speaking the Linux ABI -- zinc, the uutils family and C programs ported over ferrousli, somebody else's busybox, rustc -- and devmgr and its drivers, native programs that speak the native ABI as well, and /sbin/init, pid 1 of every image since 2026-09-26.

children.name: init
children.doc: /sbin/init (src/user/system/linux/init/, docs/INIT.md), since 2026-09-26: pid 1 around src/lib/init/svc's manager. It mounts /run and cgroup2, runs each service in a cgroup of its own from clone3, reaps, restarts, gives the console a getty and a shell with a session of its own, and powers off. /bin/svc drives it over /run/ferrix/control; it waits for notify readiness, starts services on a socket's first connection, and applies MemoryMax=, TasksMax= and OOMPolicy= over the scoped OOM kill. It gives services bootstrap channels, starts native ones in their cgroup's job, and routes the directory's OPENs. It is pid 1 of cargo xtask run and of every desktop image, where the compositor is hyprix.service and each program it starts is in a scope of its own (L10). devmgr restarts drivers by its restart policy (L11), and on an image booted with ferrix.devmgr=init pid 1 starts devmgr itself, through the kernel's starter (L12, 2026-09-27). L13, the sandboxing keys, waits for the rest of stage 13.

children.name: shell
children.doc: busybox sh was the first foreign binary to run on Ferrix: Alpine's static musl build runs a script at stage 7, given with sh -c, and cargo xtask test-shell still runs it when --init names it. The image's own shell since 2026-09-18 is zinc, whose job control cargo xtask test-jobs types at.

children.name: rustc
children.doc: The goal, stage 16, met on x86-64 on 2026-09-22: the rust-lang.org rustc, run from a btrfs volume mounted at /data, compiles hello.rs and runs what it made (cargo xtask test-rustc).

children.name: ArchFacade
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/mod.rs: the one module generic code reaches the CPU through. Each architecture exports the same set of names; the facade re-exports whichever one the build is for. Adding an architecture is a third cfg branch, not a second facade.

children.name: TLB_FLUSH_IS_BROADCAST
children.doc: True where the hardware invalidates every core's TLB in one instruction (tlbi ...is on both Arm architectures); false where the kernel has to send a shootdown IPI (x86-64).

children.name: TrapFrame
children.doc: The interrupted context as the entry stub saved it. Shape differs per machine; classify turns it into a Trap.

children.name: encoding
children.doc: PageEncoding: which src/lib/kernel/paging Encoding this machine's descriptors use.

children.name: prepareUserRoot
children.doc: Make a freshly allocated user root usable. x86-64 keeps both halves in one root, so it shares the kernel's top-level slots into it — shared, not copied, so a later kernel mapping appears in every space without walking any. The two Arm architectures do nothing: the kernel is in TTBR1.

children.name: installUserRoot
children.doc: Translate this processor's user half through a given root. x86-64 is one CR3 write, whose own side effect is to drop every non-global entry while the kernel's global ones — set because the loader enables CR4.PGE — survive. The two Arm architectures write TTBR0, clear EPD0 (the lower half is disabled rather than dismantled, so an install re-enables a regime), and then invalidate by ASID, in that order: the other order leaves the regime live with the register still naming the previous space's tables.

children.name: uninstallUserRoot
children.doc: Stop translating user addresses, which is the state a kernel thread runs in. x86-64 goes back to the kernel's own root; the Arm pair set EPD0 and invalidate, because EPD0 governs walks and not the TLB. Not lazy TLB: keeping the outgoing root installed is faster and has to keep an address space alive under a thread that holds no reference to it.

children.name: prepareStack
children.doc: Lay out a fresh task's stack so that the first switch into it "returns" into its entry function.

children.name: switchTo
children.doc: The context switch, arch/<machine>/switch.rs: saves the callee-saved set and the stack pointer, and returns onto a stack that belongs to another task, which Rust cannot say. The last entry the allow-list's every-architecture half was meant to gain.

children.name: enterUser
children.doc: enter_user: the ring-3 / EL0 / USR transition, from the program's own task, never returning. Every general register zeroed, then sysretq, eret or rfeia with interrupts open. Exceptions from user mode land on the task's own kernel stack: gs:8 and RSP0 set on each switch on x86-64, and the stack pointer at the return on the Arm pair, where SP_EL1 and the SVC stack already are that. exit_group ends the task through the scheduler.

children.name: systemCall
children.doc: The Arm half of system call entry: svc arrives through the trap vector as Trap::SystemCall, so the architecture reads the number and arguments from the saved registers, handles exit and exit_group with leave_user before dispatch, and writes the result back. x86-64's body refuses, because SYSCALL has an entry of its own.

children.name: syscallEntry
children.doc: x86-64: SYSCALL leaves the return address in rcx and does not switch the stack, so entry swaps to the kernel stack through swapgs before anything can be pushed (src/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/syscall.rs).

children.name: iommu
children.doc: The unit drivers live in src/kernel/src/iommu rather than under arch/: VT-d and the SMMUv3, each found from what the DMAR, the IORT or the device tree describes. What the facade gained for device interrupts is MSI (msi_allocate, msi_doorbell) and masking one line (mask_interrupt, unmask_interrupt).

children.name: CpuStarter
children.doc: How a secondary processor is brought from "off" to running the kernel's secondary_main with the MMU on: INIT-SIPI-SIPI and a real-mode trampoline, or PSCI CPU_ON through an identity map of the entry sequence.

children.name: X86_64Arch
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/x86_64. Target x86_64-unknown-none, kernel code model, no red zone, soft float. Machine description: ACPI.

children.name: gdt
children.doc: Per processor, with its TSS: a TSS cannot be shared because loading one marks its descriptor busy.

children.name: idt
children.doc: 256 gates, every one naming the kernel code selector; the double-fault gate on an IST stack of its own. Entry stubs are an assembler .rept, ten of which push an error code.

children.name: lapic
children.doc: Mapped from the MADT, enabled, task priority dropped. Its timer is calibrated against the HPET. One per processor.

children.name: ioapics
children.doc: Every I/O APIC firmware described is mapped and every input masked at boot; the inputs the kernel uses are routed one at a time, which is the 16550's receive interrupt, found from the MADT. Devices interrupt by MSI-X instead.

children.name: clock
children.doc: HPET main counter, whose period firmware states in femtoseconds. Falls back to the TSC calibrated against the PIT on a machine with no HPET table, and to the TSC calibrated against the HPET when its counter is 32 bits wide and would wrap every five minutes.

children.name: serial
children.doc: COM1 through port I/O. The one in-kernel device.

children.name: trampoline
children.doc: Real mode to long mode in one step, on a root table below 1 MiB sharing the kernel's upper half. The only 16-bit code in the project.

children.name: tscDeadline
children.deferred: Replaces the LAPIC countdown with a comparator against the TSC; the calibration exists. Waits for a tickless scheduler to want it.

children.name: x2apic
children.deferred: APIC IDs above 255 are refused with a message; QEMU's are 0 to 3.

children.name: vtd
children.doc: src/kernel/src/iommu/vtd.rs: legacy mode, checked against QEMU's intel_iommu.c -- a root table per unit, a context table per bus, a second-level table per domain -- programmed before PCI enumeration, so a function behind it reaches only what its domain maps. The boot test's out-of-domain write faults in the unit's fault recording register.

children.name: amdVi
children.deferred: Nothing reads an IVRS table or drives an AMD IOMMU, so on such a machine DMA would not be translated. Left after stage 10's exit: none of it was on the path to rustc.

children.name: AArch64Arch
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/aarch64. Target aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat. Machine description: ACPI (MADT, FADT for the PSCI conduit, GTDT for the timer interrupt).

children.name: vectors
children.doc: Sixteen entries at fixed 128-byte offsets; the layout is the interface. Each entry stashes two registers, records which entry it is and branches to the common save path.

children.name: gic
children.doc: aarch64/gic.rs: the MADT walk alone — distributor and CPU interface addresses, the check that every core's interface is the same banked address, the version check — then a call into the shared gicv2 driver.

children.name: timer
children.doc: The architected virtual timer, CNTV_CVAL_EL0, because a kernel at EL1 is below any hypervisor present. Compares against an absolute instant; there is no periodic mode.

children.name: serial
children.doc: Still aarch64's own copy with a hard-coded address; moving it onto the shared pl011 driver is the open half of docs/arm32.md decision 6.

children.name: psci
children.doc: Secondaries start with the MMU off at a physical address and enter through an identity map of the entry sequence alone, in a tree of their own, loading every parameter before the MMU goes on.

children.name: el2Drop
children.doc: Firmware may hand off at EL2; lowering is an eret into a constructed context.

children.name: gicv3
children.deferred: gic::init refuses anything that is not a GICv2; QEMU virt gives GICv2 unless asked, so this needs a second boot-test configuration as much as code.

children.name: parking
children.deferred: For firmware without PSCI. Refused, not guessed at.

children.name: smmu
children.doc: src/kernel/src/iommu/smmuv3.rs: every SMMUv3 the IORT describes, checked against QEMU's smmuv3.c -- a linear stream table aborting until a domain is attached, stage 2 per stream, the command queue polled and the event queue on -- with the GICv2m doorbell mapped into every domain, because QEMU sends MSI writes through the stream. The boot test's out-of-domain write faults in the event queue.

children.name: Armv7aArch
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/armv7a: the Cortex-A7 of the STM32MP157, run on QEMU virt under U-Boot. Target armv7a-none-eabi with LPAE. Machine description: device tree only. Joined after stage 3 without a second loader, a second facade or a line of bootstrap assembly; docs/arm32.md is the plan it followed.

children.name: vectors
children.doc: Eight one-instruction entries at VBAR. Each corrects the banked lr, stores it and the status on the SVC stack with srsdb and switches to SVC with cps; return is rfeia. No processor mode but SVC is ever given a stack.

children.name: gic
children.doc: Distributor and CPU interface from the device tree, then the shared gicv2 driver.

children.name: timer
children.doc: The same counter as AArch64's, reached through cp15; the interrupt number comes from the device tree.

children.name: serial
children.doc: armv7a/console.rs chooses between the ports the device tree describes, in priority order: `console=pl011|stm32` from /chosen/bootargs (U-Boot sets it without reflashing, for a board whose tree is exactly what is in question), then stdout-path, then the first enabled port. A name matching no drivable node falls through rather than failing. The PL011 on QEMU virt, the STM32 USART on the board.

children.name: coherency
children.doc: Every core reads ACTLR.SMP once it is in Rust and the boot log says how many had it set. An observation, never a failure: QEMU does not implement the register, so "clear on all" is ambiguous there. `noactlr` on the command line suppresses the read, for silicon that turns it into an undefined instruction.

children.name: psci
children.doc: Conduit from the device tree: hvc on QEMU, not the smc the plan first guessed. Secondaries found in /cpus. Entry above the 2 GiB TTBR0 covers is refused.

children.name: boardDeferred
children.deferred: The ED1 and EV1 have 1 GiB, whose identity range lands on the direct map; Layout::plan_identity_map refuses rather than guesses, so they need a trampoline page not yet written.

children.name: highRam
children.deferred: RAM beyond the 1.25 GiB direct map: a machine with it boots and reports the excess unused. RAM above the 2 GiB split, which the board's DDR at 3 GiB needs, works since 9ae0180f.

children.name: thumb2
children.deferred: ARM code generation only, as docs/arm32.md argues.

children.name: vfp
children.deferred: Soft float; a UEFI application may not assume firmware enabled the VFP.

children.name: smmu
children.deferred: The device tree's SMMUv3 is found and left alone: U-Boot's virtio-pci driver resets when a device offers VIRTIO_F_ACCESS_PLATFORM, so the machine's virtio devices would bypass it anyway, and stage 10's exit runs ARMv7-A in degraded trusted mode, as decided.

children.name: ArchLayer
children.doc: Exactly one is compiled in, chosen by the build target.

children.name: SharedArmDrivers
children.doc: Register-level drivers under arch/ shared by the two Arm architectures, gated by cfg(any(aarch64, arm)) inside the arch directory where the layering check permits it.

children.name: gicv2
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/arm_common/gicv2.rs: distributor (machine-wide) and CPU interface (per core). 0..16 software-generated, 16..32 private peripheral, 32.. shared. IPIs through GICD_SGIR. Private interrupts' enable bits are banked per core, so the driver records what the boot core enabled and init_this_cpu replays the whole set on every other core — the timer included, which is what stage 5 found missing.

children.name: pl011
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/arm_common/pl011.rs. Used by ARMv7-A today.

children.name: stm32Usart
children.doc: src/kernel/src/arch/arm_common/stm32_usart.rs: the board's own UART.

children.name: Workspace
children.doc: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §9. src/lib/ is host-testable by design and is the only code cargo test, Miri and the fuzzers can reach; src/boot/common/uefi/ and src/kernel/ are reached by the QEMU boot test; tools/common/xtask/ by cargo test. src/user/system/native/ holds the native programs the initramfs carries -- devmgr, the drivers and the runtime they link -- built for the kernel's targets and kept out of the host gates. tools/common/check/check-crate-layering.sh keeps the arrows below pointing the right way.

children.name: bootinfo
children.doc: The hand-off ABI, both address layouts, checked at compile time on every build.

children.name: elf
children.doc: ELF64 and, since the ARMv7-A port, ELF32. Used by the loader, by xtask's PE converter, and fuzzed.

children.name: heap
children.doc: The body has no unsafe; the crate cannot forbid it because declaring Backing as an unsafe trait is the point.

children.name: acpi
children.doc: Reached at stage 3: the MADT walk the interrupt controller needed. Stage 10 uses the rest: the MCFG, GICv2m frames, the DMAR and the IORT. The acpi_tables fuzz target reads its input as physical memory and walks it from the RSDP down, as the kernel does.

children.name: fdt
children.doc: Reached at stage 1 on ARMv7-A: console, GIC, timer interrupt and PSCI conduit come from it there. The fdt_parse fuzz target holds it to a second walk of the token stream written from the specification.

children.name: sync
children.doc: Reached at stage 4: its ticket locks guard every shared kernel structure, the kernel's SpinLock being PreemptSpinLock, which holds off preemption, and IrqSpinLock masking interrupts as well. SleepLock, whose waiters sleep on a wait queue the kernel lends, since stage 11. RwSpinLock still waits.

children.name: crng
children.doc: Reached with curl's HTTPS: ChaCha20 with fast key erasure behind getrandom, /dev/urandom and AT_RANDOM, seeded from firmware, the CPU and timer jitter. The block function is checked against RFC 8439 and OpenSSL's keystream.

children.name: sched
children.doc: The half of the scheduler that is arithmetic: the EEVDF tree, weights, lag, the domain partition. cargo test drives a run queue through hundreds of thousands of decisions.

children.name: vma
children.doc: Written for stage 6; reached at stage 2 as the vmap arena's range map, and since stage 6 every process's address space.

children.name: linuxAbi
children.doc: Three system call number tables, not two: x86-64's own, AArch64's generic one, and ARMv7-A's EABI one. The 32-bit architecture needs its own Syscall variants as well as its own numbers -- mmap2 counts its offset in pages, _llseek returns through a pointer, fstat64 writes a different structure -- so they are separate calls rather than the same calls renumbered. Reached early for stage 17: the DRM/KMS and evdev ioctls and layouts card0 and eventN answer, each pinned line by line to a committed UAPI probe run at both widths, and for stage 19 the virtgpu ioctls the render node answers.

children.name: ustack
children.doc: The initial process stack image: argc, argv, envp and the auxiliary vector, laid out as a program's _start reads them, at both pointer widths. Carries a reader as well as a writer, because the writer is checked by walking the bytes back out with nothing but a stack pointer -- which is also what the fuzz target does.

children.name: cpio
children.doc: The newc reader the initramfs is unpacked with, reached through src/lib/fs/vfs. The cpio_parse fuzz target writes every archive it walks to a trailer back out and requires it to read back identical.

children.name: vfs
children.doc: Dentries with negative entries, mounts, the path walk, open file descriptions, descriptor tables, tmpfs over a page store the kernel supplies, pipes and socket buffers, the permission rules as pure functions, initramfs unpacking and the getdents64 packer. The kernel's filesystem is built on it (src/kernel/src/fs).

children.name: procfs
children.doc: The text of /proc as pure functions: maps lines padded to their name column at both pointer widths, meminfo, status, stat and mounts, pinned byte for byte against lines a real Linux printed, and the maps parser the kernel's boot check reads its own output back with.

children.name: sysfs
children.doc: The text of /sys as pure functions (docs/SYSFS.md): PCI identifiers, modalias and uevent, processor lists, input capability bitmaps in words of the kernel's long, connector names, kernfs's relative link targets, and the name a write to bind or unbind gives; pinned against Linux's and fuzzed (sysfs_names).

children.name: virtio
children.doc: The split virtqueue as logic over an abstract shared memory, the PCI transport's status protocol, and each device class's own protocol: blk, net, gpu, input and console. Reached at stage 10 by the boot check's virtio-rng driver, and by every ring-3 driver since.

children.name: netwire
children.doc: The byte-level half of the net core, written ahead of the networking stage: Ethernet with one 802.1Q tag, ARP, IPv4 with its options, IPv6 with the extension-header walk, ICMPv4, ICMPv6 and Neighbor Discovery, UDP, and TCP headers with their negotiated options, each parsed without allocation and emitted into a caller's buffer, checksums verified where the format carries them. The netwire_parse fuzz target requires every header that parses to emit and parse back unchanged.

children.name: nettcp
children.doc: The TCP state machine, written ahead of the networking stage and above netwire: the eleven states of RFC 9293 in the standard's order, reassembly of what arrives out of order, window scaling, selective acknowledgment blocks, Nagle, delayed acknowledgments, silly-window avoidance and the zero-window probe, retransmission timing by RFC 6298 with Karn's algorithm, and NewReno congestion control. It holds no clock and no address: segments and a time go in, segments come out, which is what lets its tests drive two connections against each other over a wire they control. The nettcp_state fuzz target drives one connection from a stranger's segments and requires every header it answers with to write and parse back.

children.name: netCore
children.doc: The net core, written ahead of the networking stage: interfaces and the addresses on them, one routing table for both families, a neighbour cache that answers ARP's question and Neighbor Discovery's the same way, IPv4 fragmentation and reassembly under a ceiling a stranger cannot raise, ICMP echo in both directions with the unprivileged socket ping uses, UDP with Linux's socket-matching order, and TCP connections and listeners over nettcp. It holds no lock, no clock and no device: frames and a time go in and frames come out, and a packet routed to the loopback goes back into the input path rather than out of a driver. The net_input fuzz target drives a whole host from a stranger's frames.

children.name: netServe
children.doc: A ring-3 network driver's serve loop: the net ring on one side, a virtio-net device on the other, and the rules where they meet. The two directions are not symmetrical -- sending is a copy and a submission, while a frame arrives into a buffer the device chose and takes the oldest receive slot the kernel posted, or is dropped if none is waiting. A submission is never taken that cannot be answered, and a device buffer goes back the moment its bytes are copied, because a buffer the driver holds is a frame the device cannot deliver. Written against a trait, so the loop runs on the host with a fake device on one side and the ring's own kernel end on the other.

children.name: netRing
children.doc: The net ring: the memory the kernel shares with a ring-3 network driver, specified in docs/NET-RING.md. The block ring's discipline with its allocator removed: a frame is bounded by the MTU, so the data VMO is entries slots of a fixed size and a submission names its slot, which takes away the class of bug where a region is reused before its completion. Private indices, checked reads of the peer's, the want-bell handshake, and every entry checked when it is read; corruption is terminal for the side that sees it.

children.name: netlink
children.doc: The byte-level half of netlink, over linux-abi's headers: walking a buffer of messages and the attributes after each fixed header, and building replies into a caller's buffer with every length and pad computed rather than taken. Both walks refuse a length below the header it introduces, one past the end, and the zero that would walk the same message for ever, and every step forward is at least a header wide, so a walk over any bytes at all ends -- which is what lets the kernel read a buffer a program wrote. It allocates nothing, so a whole dump is encoded inside the lock over the net core. The netlink_walk fuzz target requires the walk to end, what it borrows to lie inside the input, and anything the builder writes to walk back to what was built.

children.name: virtioNet
children.doc: The virtio-net driver logic, written ahead of the network device it drives from src/user/system/native/drivers/net/virtio-net: bring-up in the order the status protocol fixes, a receive queue the driver fills and refills because an empty one drops every frame in silence, a transmit queue whose buffers stay the caller's until the device says it has read them, and a drain that acknowledges the interrupt before it starts. It negotiates no checksum, segmentation or merge-buffer feature, so a frame is one buffer and every header is the twelve bytes VERSION_1 makes it. It holds no handle: a transport, pinned pages and a header area go in, and frames go each way. The virtio_net fuzz target drives it from a device whose every register, used entry and header byte a stranger chose, and requires every accepted frame to be answered exactly once.

children.name: virtioGpu
children.doc: The virtio-gpu 2D driver logic, written ahead of the driver process for the compositor's first iteration and driven from src/user/system/native/drivers/display/virtio-gpu since: bring-up with the control queue alone, one command at a time, every response checked, and the pipeline from the display core's requests to device commands. A failed step is undone as far as is safe, and pages the device may still hold are never unpinned. Its tests drive a frame to a fake device's screen; the virtio_gpu_pipeline fuzz target requires one reply per request and no unpin without a pin. Since stage 19 it takes the features 3D needs when asked.

children.name: virtioSnd
children.doc: The virtio-snd driver logic, written ahead of the driver process for the audio iteration (docs/AUDIO.md L4): bring-up with DRIVER_OK before HELLO, since a sound device describes its streams only through its control queue; READY into SET_PARAMS and PREPARE; one transmit chain per SUBMIT, the header and status from the driver's scratch memory and the samples from the core's buffer pinned read-only; completions back to the core oldest first; a halt as STOP, RELEASE and a fresh prepare. Tested against a device doing what QEMU 9.2.4's does, with the samples the device read compared to those submitted.

children.name: virtioInput
children.doc: The virtio-input driver logic, written ahead of the driver process for the input iteration (docs/INPUT.md) and driven from src/user/system/native/drivers/input/virtio-input since: bring-up that stops at FEATURES_OK so no event is discarded before the core has judged the device, the device's description read as a HELLO, the event queue kept full because QEMU drops a whole report for want of one buffer, and the events the device wrote batched into the EVENTS messages the core reads. It forwards only what the core would publish and drops the rest; it ends a report the core would refuse for length and counts the cut; and memory the device may still write into is never handed back. The virtio_input_driver fuzz target plays a device and the glue against a real session, and requires the core never to refuse a message the batch made and no event to be lost or reordered.

children.name: displayctl
children.doc: The control protocol between the kernel's display core and a ring-3 display driver, written ahead of both for the compositor's first iteration (docs/DISPLAY.md). Frames do not move -- the card VMO's ranges are the device's backing, or since stage 19 a GPU object ATTACH_OBJECT names -- so there is no ring, only thirteen fixed messages decoded strictly, and the core's side of the conversation as a state machine of fixed capacity that accepts only the reply it waits for and stays broken once a driver lies. The displayctl fuzz target requires decoding to be exact and the session never to accept a flip out of order.

children.name: inputctl
children.doc: The control protocol between the kernel's input core and a ring-3 input driver, and evdev's per-open queues, written ahead of both for the input iteration (docs/INPUT.md). Six fixed messages decoded strictly; the core's side of the conversation, which publishes only the event types it supports, refuses a message holding any event the driver did not declare before any of it takes effect, keeps the device state as Linux's input_get_disposition does and delivers whole reports to the grabbing open or to all; and the queue, Linux evdev's ring with its SYN_DROPPED rule, packet boundary, flush on a state read and clock change, read as input_event at both widths. The inputctl fuzz target requires decoding to be exact, every delivered report whole and published, and every drained read to end at a SYN_REPORT with its clean reports the ones delivered, in order.

children.name: sndctl
children.doc: The control protocol between the kernel's audio core and a ring-3 sound driver, and a PCM stream's state as ALSA keeps it, written ahead of both for the audio iteration (docs/AUDIO.md L3). Nine fixed messages decoded strictly; the core's side of the conversation, which publishes the first stream that plays version 1's one configuration and refuses any report out of turn; the stream, Linux's pcm_native.c and pcm_lib.c function by function: states, pointers and boundary at both widths, thresholds, start, underrun, drain, SYNC_PTR, STATUS and poll, with what is submitted to the driver and when; and HW_REFINE and HW_PARAMS with Linux's interval and mask rules. The sndctl fuzz target drives requests, completions and lies at a stream and requires it never to overrun, never to submit across a period or during a halt, and to refuse every lie.

children.name: logctl
children.doc: The log control protocol: how a ring-3 driver reads the kernel log over a control channel, for the Pixel 7's USB serial port (docs/vendor/google/pixel7/USB-HANDOVER.md phase 4). Three messages decoded strictly -- READ, DATA with the bytes the ring lost since the last, REFUSED -- and the kernel's half of the conversation: one READ outstanding, answered once the log has a byte, lost counts carried to the next DATA.

children.name: audit
children.doc: The audit record's 64-byte layout, shared by the kernel's store (src/kernel/src/audit.rs) and the reader it hands the records to (docs/certification/AUDIT.md §2): the classes, the events, the configuration keys, and the start-up record that carries the boot's 128-bit audit id and both ring lengths, round-tripped through the bytes by its host tests.

children.name: pci
children.doc: PCI configuration space over a ConfigSpace the caller implements: ECAM geometry, headers, BAR decoding and sizing, both capability lists with a visited set, MSI-X, the bus walk without recursion or allocation, and virtio's PCI transport. The kernel's enumeration walks with it (src/kernel/src/discovery/pci.rs). The pci_walk fuzz target requires every walk to end and sizing to restore every register.

children.name: nativeAbi
children.doc: The native ABI's numbers, handle values, rights, signals, errno names and repr(C) layouts. One table on every architecture, in 0x1000..=0x1FFF, tested clear of all three Linux tables. No argument wider than a register.

children.name: objects
children.doc: The handle table and the channel message queue, generic over what a handle names. A handle is a slot and a generation, and a slot retires rather than wrap, so a closed handle never resolves again -- which the handle_table fuzz target checks against a model.

children.name: btrfs
children.doc: The btrfs read path, allocating nothing: parsing, mount bootstrap, lookup, readdir and read with every data sector checked against the checksum tree, and zlib, LZO and zstd decoders. Tested against real mkfs.btrfs images, fuzzed from them by btrfs_read, and mounted by the kernel since stage 11.

children.name: btrfsWrite
children.doc: The btrfs write path: copy-on-write trees, delayed refs, extent and free-space-tree bookkeeping, chunk allocation, the commit with its flush before the superblock, file operations, and the log tree fsync writes and the mount replays. Host btrfs check finds its output clean, both from host tests and from what the kernel writes in the boot check, and after power failures cut at thousands of points on the host and hundreds of QEMU kills.

children.name: btrfsVfs
children.doc: btrfs mounted into the VFS: FileSystem and Inode over the read path, read-only and holding no lock across I/O, and a writable mount over src/lib/fs/btrfs-write behind one sleeping lock, whose writes become extents at the commit.

children.name: blockQueue
children.doc: The block core's request queue: merging, flush and FUA barriers no request crosses, deadline scheduling. In front of every block ring in the kernel (src/kernel/src/interfaces/block_ring). Checked against a model by the block_queue fuzz target.

children.name: blkRing
children.doc: The block ring, docs/BLOCK-RING.md in code: the memory the kernel shares with a ring-3 block driver, every index and entry the other side writes checked before it is used, doorbells over ports, and the HELLO, READY and START messages, linked by both the kernel's ring glue and the driver. The blkring fuzz target plays one side against an honest other.

children.name: blkServe
children.doc: A ring-3 block driver's serve loop between the block ring and a virtio-blk device, written against a trait so it runs on the host with a fake device; src/user/system/native/drivers/block/virtio-blk adds only the handles.

children.name: virtioBlk
children.doc: The virtio-blk driver logic over a transport and DMA memory it is handed: bring-up to DRIVER_OK, read, write and flush, each completion counted once even from a hostile device, and memory handed back only after the device's reset. Driven from src/user/system/native/drivers/block/virtio-blk; fuzzed by virtio_blk.

children.name: devmgrProto
children.doc: The messages between the kernel and devmgr on its bootstrap channel as docs/DEVMGR.md fixes them -- DEVICES, REPORT, PUBLISHED, DIED and RESTARTED -- so the kernel and the program share one definition.

children.name: nativeCrate
children.doc: Typed, safe wrappers over every native system call, with owned handles, written against a raw call trait: src/user/system/native/rt implements it with the trap instruction, and the tests with a recorder that plays the kernel's part.

children.name: renderctl
children.doc: The render control protocol between the kernel's render core and a ring-3 GPU driver (docs/GPU.md §3.3), in displayctl's shape: fixed messages decoded strictly, command buffers passed through as bytes the driver understands and the core does not, and the core's side as a state machine. Fuzzed by renderctl.

children.name: gc400
children.doc: The STM32MP157's Vivante GC400T as logic over registers and command memory (docs/GPU.md §6.3): the registers and the command stream from the etnaviv project's MIT-licensed register database, the identity, reset and initialisation in the order Linux's etnaviv driver uses them, and a WAIT/LINK ring. Linked by src/user/system/native/drivers/gpu/gc400, which devmgr starts on the board, where it ran on 2026-09-24; no QEMU machine has the core, so no gate drives it.

children.name: fbtext
children.doc: Text and filled rectangles on a linear framebuffer, with an embedded Spleen 8x16 font, clipped rather than refused and allocating nothing: what the panic screen (src/kernel/src/panic/screen.rs) draws with, and src/user/system/linux/compositor/term as well.

children.name: qr
children.doc: A QR code encoder with no heap, ported from Linux's drm_panic_qr.rs, for the panic screen's report.

children.name: vdagent
children.doc: SPICE's vdagent protocol as bytes, the chunk framing and the clipboard messages (docs/CLIPBOARD.md §4). Written ahead of the clipboard agent; since 2026-09-27 that agent, src/user/system/linux/compositor/vdagent, speaks it, and cargo xtask test-clipboard drives it both ways.

children.name: virtioConsole
children.doc: The virtio-console driver: bring-up, the control conversation until a named port is open, and that port's bytes (docs/CLIPBOARD.md §3). Linked by src/user/system/native/drivers/console/vport, which devmgr starts when --clipboard puts the device on the bus; cargo xtask test-clipboard drives it (2026-09-27).

children.name: seccompBpf
children.doc: The classic-BPF interpreter as a pure function over bytes.

children.name: xtask
children.doc: Cross-compiles both halves and the native programs, writes the FAT32 image and the initramfs with its own writers, converts the ARMv7-A loader ELF to PE32, drives QEMU, runs the NAT gateway the network tests sit behind, and runs every gate. Nothing from crates.io. It no longer forbids unsafe: a few calls into Windows, for the console and an ICMP echo, each with its SAFETY comment.

children.name: MemKind
children.doc: Firmware's memory types folded into what the kernel cares about. Usable is free at boot; Loader and AcpiReclaim are reclaimable once nothing points into them; Reserved, Mmio and Defective are not RAM.

children.name: Framebuffer
children.doc: True when the framebuffer is in memory the frame allocator will own (UEFI virtio-gpu's boot-services framebuffer): the panic screen does not draw on it and the display core reads it before publishing a card.

children.name: BootInfo
children.doc: Version 4. Every type is repr(C); the kernel refuses to start if the magic or version disagree. Addresses are u64 on every width so the layout is one layout. The kernel validates it once through BootInfo::validate into a BootView whose accessors are safe.

children.name: regions
children.doc: Sorted, non-overlapping, describing the loader's own allocations — without which the frame allocator would hand out the frames holding its own page tables.

children.name: physmapPhys
children.doc: The direct map begins at the lowest RAM address rather than at zero: a gibibyte in on QEMU's Arm machines.

children.name: dtbLen
children.doc: The device tree is copied into memory of its own kind, DeviceTree, so it outlives the reclaim of firmware's copy; stage 10 enumerates devices from the same bytes.

children.name: cmdline
children.doc: key=value options and bare flags, one grammar (option_in, flag_in) whether the loader filled this in or the kernel read /chosen/bootargs from the device tree, which is where the Arm boards carry it. Options today: console=pl011|stm32, nosmp (describe_cpus returns the boot CPU only), noactlr, ferrix.onexit=reset (a board resets rather than powering off), ferrix.root=tmpfs (/ stays in memory), ferrix.checks=skip|run (stages 2 to 12 brought up without their self-checks, for a desktop), and ferrix.btrfs with ferrix.btrfs.seed for the power-fail test. The loader reads the card owner's /FERRIX/CMDLINE.TXT and then the image's /FERRIX/DEFAULTS.TXT, joined, so the owner's value of a key comes first and wins.

children.name: VirtualLayout
children.doc: src/lib/proto/bootinfo::Layout. Both instances are checked for overlap at compile time on every build, whichever one the build uses.

children.name: vmapReserved
children.doc: The front of the vmap area held back for fixed windows — the framebuffer and the demand-paging test window — before the arena begins.

children.name: layout64
